content: An enamel rod, also referred to as an enamel prism in older terminology, represents the fundamental structural unit of enamel. Each enamel rod measures approximately 4 micrometers in width and 8 micrometers in height. It is composed of a densely packed and highly organized assembly of hydroxyapatite crystals. When viewed in cross-section, an enamel rod resembles a keyhole shape. The head of the keyhole is oriented toward the crown of the tooth, while the tail is directed toward the root of the tooth. Enamel rods are arranged in rows along the surface of the tooth. Within each row, the long axis of the enamel rod is generally perpendicular to the underlying dentin. In permanent teeth, the enamel rods near the cementoenamel junction (CEJ) exhibit a slight inclination toward the root of the tooth, deviating from the expected perpendicular orientation. This specific orientation of enamel is critical in restorative dentistry, as enamel that lacks support from the underlying dentin is more susceptible to fracture and is typically avoided during dental procedures. The internal structure of each enamel rod is highly intricate. The hydroxyapatite crystals within the rod are predominantly aligned parallel to its long axis. However, as the crystals extend further from the central axis of the rod, their orientation begins to diverge. Surrounding each enamel rod is a region known as interrod enamel. Although interrod enamel shares the same chemical composition as the enamel rods, it is histologically distinct due to differences in the orientation of the crystals. In interrod enamel, the crystals are arranged nearly perpendicular to those within the enamel rod.
